items.abstract: Global Civilizational Equilibrium Doctrine 2026 (GCED-26) Version 2.0 — Complete Twelve-Volume Governance and Systems Framework GCED-26 Version 2.0 presents a twelve-volume interdisciplinary governance and systems framework for the structured design, analysis, modelling, evaluation, documentation, and potential implementation of long-horizon civilizational governance architectures. The framework addresses civilizational equilibrium, institutional coordination, legal and constitutional boundaries, mathematical and systems stability, artificial intelligence and algorithmic governance, planetary resources and ecological systems, economic and monetary coordination, strategic stability and non-domination, digital infrastructure and cyber resilience, human rights and social equity, verification and validation methodologies, and evidence-gated implementation pathways. GCED-26 is an independent, copyrighted, and licensed governance and systems framework. It is not presented as a peer-reviewed academic publication, governmental standard, treaty, statute, judicial decision, intergovernmental instrument, or source of binding legal authority. Its institutional, legal, mathematical, computational, technological, economic, ecological, strategic, and implementation components are presented according to their respective methodological status and stated assumptions. The framework distinguishes normative propositions, descriptive analysis, legal analysis, mathematical claims, computational results, empirical evidence, institutional proposals, policy proposals, and implementation procedures. No category is treated as automatically establishing another. Mathematical formalization does not by itself establish legal authority, political legitimacy, empirical truth, institutional competence, or operational feasibility. Computational simulation does not by itself constitute mathematical proof, empirical validation, or evidence of real-world governance performance. I. CORE DOCTRINE & FOUNDATIONS The foundational volume establishes the conceptual, analytical, methodological, and systems architecture of GCED-26. It addresses: Civilizational equilibrium and systemic coordination Definitions and terminology Foundational axioms and principles System boundaries and state variables Equilibrium and constrained equilibrium Multi-objective equilibrium Pareto efficiency and non-domination Resilience and stability Governance safety constraints Institutional design foundations Information and evidence architecture Uncertainty classification Reproducibility architecture Validation methodology Formal research and analytical questions Canonical mathematical notation Computational reference models Cross-volume dependencies Scope conditions Limitations Research and analytical integrity The volume establishes clear distinctions among conceptual doctrine, normative principles, mathematical formalization, empirical evidence, institutional design, legal authority, computational implementation, and policy implementation. The foundational architecture treats civilizational governance as a complex, multi-domain, constrained, uncertain, and interconnected systems problem rather than as a single-variable optimization problem or a centralized command structure. II. INTERNATIONAL LEGAL & CONSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK The second volume examines the international legal and constitutional conditions relevant to proposed governance architectures. It addresses: Sources and structure of international law Sovereignty Jurisdiction Competence and lawful authority Human rights and fundamental freedoms Equality and non-discrimination Due process and procedural safeguards Treaty architecture Constitutional design principles Institutional accountability Separation of powers Compliance and monitoring Evidence and attribution Algorithmic decision-making boundaries Dispute settlement Judicial and administrative review Remedies and appeals Emergency powers Necessity and proportionality Transition and legal validation Jurisdictional limitations Institutional authorization requirements Existing international legal instruments are distinguished from proposed GCED-26 arrangements. Reference to an international treaty, declaration, convention, principle, institution, or legal doctrine does not by itself create legal force for GCED-26, establish jurisdiction, impose treaty obligations, create constitutional authority, or confer institutional competence. A proposed governance measure is treated as legally operational only where the applicable legal order provides an appropriate legal basis, competent authority, jurisdiction, procedure, rights safeguards, accountability mechanism, and review or remedy pathway. III. INSTITUTIONAL & GLOBAL GOVERNANCE ARCHITECTURE The third volume develops a proposed institutional architecture for coordinated governance subject to defined competence, accountability, legal boundaries, review, transparency, and separation of functions. It addresses: Institutional architecture Competence allocation Global coordination mechanisms Proposed Global Equilibrium Council (GEC) Coordination and monitoring functions Proposed Civilizational Stability Authority (CSA) Adjudication and judicial review Resource governance institutions AI and technology governance Appointment and removal procedures Separation of institutional functions Oversight and audit Transparency Conflict-of-interest controls Inter-institutional coordination Emergency governance Sunset provisions Rollback mechanisms Accountability Institutional review Delegated authority Competence boundaries Institutional failure containment Institutional bodies proposed within GCED-26 are treated as design proposals, not as existing international institutions or independent sources of legal authority. The institutional architecture does not presume that coordination requires centralized sovereignty. Authority is differentiated according to competence, jurisdiction, procedural safeguards, accountability, review, and applicable legal constraints. IV. MATHEMATICAL & SYSTEMS STABILITY THEORY The fourth volume provides the mathematical framework for analysing equilibrium, stability, uncertainty, robustness, controlled dynamical systems, and constrained multi-objective systems. items.abstract: Global Civilizational Equilibrium Doctrine 2026 (GCED-26) Version 2.0 — Complete Twelve-Volume Governance and Systems Framework GCED-26 Version 2.0 presents a twelve-volume interdisciplinary governance and systems framework for the structured design, analysis, modelling, evaluation, documentation, and potential implementation of long-horizon civilizational governance architectures. The framework addresses civilizational equilibrium, institutional coordination, legal and constitutional boundaries, mathematical and systems stability, artificial intelligence and algorithmic governance, planetary resources and ecological systems, economic and monetary coordination, strategic stability and non-domination, digital infrastructure and cyber resilience, human rights and social equity, verification and validation methodologies, and evidence-gated implementation pathways. GCED-26 is an independent, copyrighted, and licensed governance and systems framework. It is not presented as a peer-reviewed academic publication, governmental standard, treaty, statute, judicial decision, intergovernmental instrument, or source of binding legal authority. Its institutional, legal, mathematical, computational, technological, economic, ecological, strategic, and implementation components are presented according to their respective methodological status and stated assumptions. The framework distinguishes normative propositions, descriptive analysis, legal analysis, mathematical claims, computational results, empirical evidence, institutional proposals, policy proposals, and implementation procedures. No category is treated as automatically establishing another. Mathematical formalization does not by itself establish legal authority, political legitimacy, empirical truth, institutional competence, or operational feasibility. Computational simulation does not by itself constitute mathematical proof, empirical validation, or evidence of real-world governance performance. I. CORE DOCTRINE & FOUNDATIONS The foundational volume establishes the conceptual, analytical, methodological, and systems architecture of GCED-26. It addresses: Civilizational equilibrium and systemic coordination Definitions and terminology Foundational axioms and principles System boundaries and state variables Equilibrium and constrained equilibrium Multi-objective equilibrium Pareto efficiency and non-domination Resilience and stability Governance safety constraints Institutional design foundations Information and evidence architecture Uncertainty classification Reproducibility architecture Validation methodology Formal research and analytical questions Canonical mathematical notation Computational reference models Cross-volume dependencies Scope conditions Limitations Research and analytical integrity The volume establishes clear distinctions among conceptual doctrine, normative principles, mathematical formalization, empirical evidence, institutional design, legal authority, computational implementation, and policy implementation. The foundational architecture treats civilizational governance as a complex, multi-domain, constrained, uncertain, and interconnected systems problem rather than as a single-variable optimization problem or a centralized command structure. II. INTERNATIONAL LEGAL & CONSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK The second volume examines the international legal and constitutional conditions relevant to proposed governance architectures. It addresses: Sources and structure of international law Sovereignty Jurisdiction Competence and lawful authority Human rights and fundamental freedoms Equality and non-discrimination Due process and procedural safeguards Treaty architecture Constitutional design principles Institutional accountability Separation of powers Compliance and monitoring Evidence and attribution Algorithmic decision-making boundaries Dispute settlement Judicial and administrative review Remedies and appeals Emergency powers Necessity and proportionality Transition and legal validation Jurisdictional limitations Institutional authorization requirements Existing international legal instruments are distinguished from proposed GCED-26 arrangements. III. INSTITUTIONAL & GLOBAL GOVERNANCE ARCHITECTURE The third volume develops a proposed institutional architecture for coordinated governance subject to defined competence, accountability, legal boundaries, review, transparency, and separation of functions. items.title: Global transportation impacts on wildlife mortality and emerging pathways for mitigation
items.abstract: Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine transportation are fundamental to modern human life, but vehicle collisions with wildlife inadvertently kill hundreds of millions of animals across 2000 vertebrate and invertebrate species annually; however, a comprehensive framework to assess and mitigate these mortalities is missing. We identified and compared the most up-to-date information regarding the impacts of transportation on wildlife mortality to determine cross-cutting solutions to this challenging problem. For example, numerous strategies, such as under- or overpasses traversing roads and railways that increase wildlife-habitat connectivity, policies that enforce reduced speed in areas with active wildlife, and passive sensors that detect wildlife to alert nearby ships and vehicles and enable mandatory speed reductions, can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions. We explored emerging technological advances that could help further reduce future wildlife-vehicle conflicts and provide a path forward for transportation systems. Specifically, we described how the combination of citizen science, artificial intelligence, targeted studies on wildlife demographic impacts, and cost-effective mitigation efforts will be powerful tools to inform needed future policies to decrease ship speed in areas with threatened whale species and reduce rates of wildlife mortality across ecosystems in a fast-moving world.

items.title: Governing AI Outputs in a Fully Sensed Society: Is Output Governance Sufficient for Social Acceptance?
items.abstract: Advances in sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are moving smart cities toward a Fully Sensed Society (FSS), in which human behavior and states can be continuously inferred. This paper presents the Fully Monitored Public Space (FMPS) as a scaled-down model of the FSS and a smart-city testbed, and examines two questions. First, to what extent can unauthorized external AI outputs be structurally deterred? The previously proposed Verifiable Record of AI Output (VRAIO) binds outputs to Rules, an independent Recorder, tamper-resistant records, audits, and sanctions, making deviations verifiable and attributable. The Recorder, however, checks only the consistency of declared metadata with the Rules, not the output content; false declarations are deterred because unannounced audits and sanctions make their expected benefit smaller than the expected loss upon detection. Second, if such trustworthiness is secured, does it lead to social acceptance of being continuously known by AI? We propose a staged and reversible evaluation framework for the FMPS that distinguishes acceptance grounded in the experience of “no actual harm” and of “benefits” (personal and social) from resignation accompanied by chilling effects. This paper does not answer the question; it presents a method for asking it empirically.

items.title: GraphOPD: Graph-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for LLM Agents
items.abstract: On-policy distillation post-trains large language model agents by supplying dense, step-level guidance from a teacher policy when the reinforcement-learning reward is sparse and arrives only once per trajectory. Existing instantiations allocate this guidance by the size of the teacher-student divergence at each step, on the single-turn intuition that a large disagreement marks a mistake worth correcting. Once decisions chain over many turns, that rule misfires, since an early drift enters every later context both policies condition on, leaving the teacher consistent with the drifted trajectory instead of flagging its cause, while interchangeable steps register large but outcome-irrelevant divergences. We demonstrate this on an agentic benchmark, where distilling the highest-divergence steps brings no consistent benefit over random selection. To this end, we introduce GraphOPD, the first method to bring graph-based structural augmentation into on-policy distillation for agent capabilities. It reads which steps enabled which later ones from the environment's own record of state changes, immune to the drift that corrupts the teacher-student gap, organizes them into a dependency graph, scores each step by a random-walk stationary distribution over it, and fuses that structural credit with the divergence signal into a trajectory-relative mask concentrating supervision on each rollout's highest-aptitude steps. Across three model scales and eleven baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA, GraphOPD shows competitive performance throughout, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +5.8 pp. An executed-replay audit further shows that this structural credit score tracks true causal impact far above chance, that both fused signals are independently necessary, and that the same signal transfers to out-of-domain tool-integrated reasoning.

items.title: Grounded but Wrong: Claim–Computation Binding Catches Spoofable Provenance in Agentic Statistical Analysis
items.abstract: We present a claim–computation binding audit: a deterministic instrument that verifies whether each claim in an AI-generated analysis is bound to the executed tool call that produced its statistic, classifying each binding (errored / variable-mismatch / stat-mismatch / clean), together with the keyed ground-truth benchmark and the pre-registered, provenance-stamped run corpora on which we ablate it. The setting is agentic statistical root-cause analysis (the Analyze phase of Six Sigma DMAIC), where the trust signals practitioners rely on prove gameable: a no-LLM fill-in-the-blanks template scores 0.867 on a completeness rubric with verified-recall 0, so "complete and well-cited" measures form, not correctness. Applying the audit to a pre-hardening corpus of agentic DMAIC runs (n=23 supported claims, 3 small open-weight models), 52.2% of supported claims (12/23) carry a binding defect even though audit-ID provenance resolves 100%; 6/23 (~26%) are the motivating subclass, a claim citing a real, audit-logged statistic that actually concerns different variables. We call such provenance spoofable. In a pre-registered ablation (180 runs; 45 pairs per contrast; hash-frozen scoring and binding code), the full 12-safeguard stack (base-6 artifact-hygiene checks plus our six correctness safeguards D1–D6, anchored by the claim–computation binding check D1) cuts the run-level binding-defect rate from 28.9% to 2.2% (Holm-corrected p=0.0055). The contrasts isolating single components are not significant (D1–D5: directionally consistent, Holm-corrected p=0.1406; D6: uninformative, 1/45 vs 0/45), so the confirmed effect is stack-level. Descriptively, 9 of the 13 unguarded defective runs are MISSING-only, a class an artifact-existence check can already catch, while the semantic classes (wrong variables, mismatched statistics, or unverifiable statistics; this paper's motivating phenomenon) fall from 4/45 to 0/45 under the full stack. The design was not power-analyzed, and discovery shows no detectable improvement (95% CI on the paired difference spans zero): the safeguards reduce fabricated support, not analytical error. Defects are rarer at larger scale (1/15 unguarded runs at each of a 32B and a frontier-family model, both exploratory) but do not vanish, and binding cleanliness holds on a sealed held-out pair. We contribute a measurement that separates grounded from correct, a detector for spoofable provenance, an honestly-bounded safeguard, and an artifact bundle containing the pre-registration with hash-frozen analysis code, per-run score and binding tables for all five corpora, and per-run summaries (provenance-stamped for the four pre-registered corpora).

items.title: Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) equipped with terminal access have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating software engineering tasks. However, existing agents remain brittle on long-horizon workflows, where they must repeatedly reconstruct program state scattered across source files, configurations, tests, dependencies, and runtime behavior, leading to increasingly long interaction histories, context explosion, and semantic drift. Large repositories further complicate the identification of task-relevant components. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{Dev-Primitives} (\emph{Development Primitives}), a modular and executable abstraction that transforms repository components from passive software artifacts into active participants in software engineering. Each Dev-Primitive pairs a repository artifact with a resident LLM, which gives the artifact an agent-native interface grounded in its own implementation and dependencies, enabling natural-language reasoning, inter-component communication, and localized self-modification. Building on Dev-Primitives, we propose \textbf{HERMES}, a Harness Engineering framework for software engineeRing via Modular Executable Dev-PrimitiveS, which instantiates these primitives at repository scale through a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to the components that must be revised. Extensive experiments on four software engineering benchmarks demonstrate that HERMES outperforms matched baseline harnesses by 12.4\% on average. Moreover, when paired with strong activation and diagnosis models, HERMES, even with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, remains within 4.5\% of the homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol configuration across all four benchmarks, while reducing inference cost by 26.2\% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, highlighting the importance of harness design in software engineering agents.

items.title: Harnessing the potential of artificial intelligence for transformative healthcare solutions
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the important catalysts to change the practice of healthcare through availability for better patient care, greater efficiency in clinical workflow, and progress in medical research. There will be further discussion concerning machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics wherein the result will be better decision-making, fewer errors, and an increase in operational efficiency. In addition to this, there will be discussion concerning challenges that are faced, such as privacy issues, ethical issues, and integration with preexisting healthcare infrastructure and the implications that the future of AI-based solutions indicates. This work will synthesize contemporary trends in healthcare, case studies, and the technological applications that have been evolved to explore the important part that AI will have as it continues to develop in creating a more efficient, accurate, and patient-centered system of healthcare delivery.

items.title: Hiding Tool Latency in On-Device Cascaded Voice Agent through Speculative Execution
items.abstract: Tool-augmented speech assistants typically serialize automatic speech recognition, large language model inference, and external tool execution. As a result, tool latency is incurred only after the user has finished speaking and the LLM has identified the required tool calls. We present speculative tool execution for on-device cascaded voice agents, which predicts tool requests from partial ASR hypotheses and initiates tool execution while speech is still being received, thereby reducing end-to-end response latency. Our approach introduces a Predictor module that anticipates tool calls during speech recognition, executes them speculatively, and caches the results. The cached outputs are then injected into the LLM prompt, enabling faster responses. Additionally, to mitigate errors caused by user self-corrections during speech, we employ a rule-based validation mechanism that selectively injects only valid cached results. As a final safeguard, the LLM retains the ability to issue tool calls directly, ensuring that the latency of our framework is upper-bounded by the baseline serial execution pipeline in the worst case. We evaluate our method using live measurements from a fully implemented Android voice assistant. Our approach reduces the median time-to-first-audio from 5.79,s to 4.60,s and decreases the standard deviation from 3.49,s to 2.81,s, resulting in more predictable response latency.

items.title: HiPLEX: Hierarchical Policy Factorization for Full Duplex Speech Language Models
items.abstract: As human--AI interactions become more conversational, full-duplex speech language models capable of natural real-time dialogue are growing in importance. Beyond generating appropriate responses, these models must coordinate turn-taking, backchanneling, and floor management in real time. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a way to refine these behaviors through direct feedback on interaction outcomes. However, existing RL methods either apply timing feedback to a token policy or optimize semantic content, leaving the joint improvement of timing and content unresolved. We introduce HiPLEX, an RL framework that factorizes a pretrained full-duplex text policy into a control policy that decides when to emit content and a conditional content policy that decides what to emit. The first factor selects among 'pad', 'epad', and 'con'. The second selects a token only when 'con' is chosen. This hierarchy describes conditional actions within each frame and uses the model's existing text head. We route timing advantages to the token-group factor through event-causal masks derived from generated speech episodes, and route an LLM-judge semantic advantage to the conditional content factor. items.title: Horizons and Emerging Possibilities for the New Academic Wave
items.abstract: Each of the preceding chapters in this book has, in one way or another, explored a transformation already in progress. This chapter turns instead to what lies ahead. The reflections offered here are grounded in the evidence, patterns, and analytical commitments developed throughout the earlier chapters, yet they are presented as plausible trajectories rather than firm predictions. This chapter explores four interconnected developments shaping the future of higher education. It examines artificial intelligence (AI) as it expands beyond teaching and learning into institutional strategy, governance, and administration, within the evolving regulatory frameworks of the European Union and United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO). It analyses immersive learning through virtual and augmented reality, highlighting that its impact depends less on technology itself than on infrastructure, staff readiness, and equitable access. The chapter then investigates the rise of the networked university, where platform-based collaborations and models such as micro-campuses are redefining institutional boundaries while raising new questions about power and inequality. Finally, it considers micro-credentials and digital credentialling, including blockchain-based systems, emphasising that their credibility rests on robust governance and quality assurance. Across these developments, a common theme emerges: technology does not determine educational outcomes. Its effects, whether expanding opportunity or reinforcing existing divides, depend on institutional choices, leadership, and ethical governance. The chapter concludes that the future of higher education will be shaped not primarily by technological innovation, but by the capacity of institutions and stakeholders to govern change deliberately, responsibly, and strategically.

items.title: How a Data Analytics Course in Kolkata Helps Learners Master Power BI and Business Analytics
items.abstract: Businesses today generate vast amounts of information through sales transactions, customer interactions, marketing campaigns, financial operations, websites and digital platforms. The challenge is no longer simply collecting this information. Organisations need professionals who can transform complex datasets into understandable reports, identify meaningful patterns and support business decisions with evidence. This is where Power BI and business analytics have become increasingly valuable. Microsoft Power BI enables professionals to connect data sources, transform information, build data models and create interactive dashboards that communicate business performance. Business analytics adds another layer by helping organisations interpret those findings and use them for planning and decision-making. The Growing Importance of Analytics Skills The Indian employment market is undergoing a significant technology-driven transformation. Recent reporting from the Times of India highlights that artificial intelligence is putting pressure on repetitive and outdated technology roles while increasing demand for professionals with skills in areas such as AI, data science, cloud computing and machine learning. This shift is making data-related capabilities increasingly relevant across industries. Organisations need professionals who can work with information, understand business requirements and communicate insights effectively. The demand is also visible in current hiring patterns. Recent job listings show Power BI being combined with skills such as SQL, DAX, Power Query, data modelling and ETL, demonstrating that modern business intelligence roles increasingly require a broader analytical toolkit rather than dashboard creation alone. For learners, this creates an opportunity to build a combination of technical and business skills through a data analytics course in Kolkata. Understanding the Role of Power BI Power BI is widely used for business intelligence and data visualisation. Its value comes from the ability to bring information from different sources into an environment where it can be transformed, analysed and presented. A typical Power BI workflow can involve importing information from spreadsheets or databases, cleaning the data, creating relationships between datasets, developing calculations and presenting the final results through interactive reports. This process teaches an important lesson in analytics: a dashboard is only as useful as the data and reasoning behind it. Learners need to understand the business purpose of each report, select appropriate metrics and ensure that the information presented is accurate and meaningful. A data analytics course in Kolkata can introduce learners to this complete workflow rather than treating Power BI as simply a chart-making application. Building a Strong Foundation Before Dashboard Development Effective Power BI work begins before the dashboard itself is created. Learners first need to understand data structures, data types, data quality and basic analytical concepts. Business datasets may contain duplicate records, missing values, inconsistent naming conventions or incorrect formats. Cleaning and preparing such information is therefore an essential stage of analytics. Power Query can help automate many data preparation and transformation activities. Learning these processes allows learners to create cleaner datasets before developing reports. This foundation is important because a visually attractive dashboard cannot compensate for unreliable underlying information. Developing Data Modelling Skills Data modelling is another important part of business intelligence. Organisations often have information stored across different tables and systems. Connecting these datasets correctly allows analysts to create more comprehensive reports. Learners can develop an understanding of relationships, dimensions, measures and structured data models. This helps them create reports that remain reliable as datasets become more complex. DAX, or Data Analysis Expressions, is also important for creating calculations and measures within Power BI. Developing familiarity with DAX can help learners move beyond basic visualisation towards more sophisticated analytical reporting. These capabilities are particularly relevant because current Power BI roles frequently mention DAX, Power Query, SQL, ETL and data modelling alongside dashboard development. Turning Dashboards into Business Intelligence The real value of Power BI appears when dashboards answer meaningful business needs. For example, a sales dashboard could show revenue by region, product category and month. A marketing dashboard could track campaign performance, customer acquisition and conversion rates. A financial report could monitor expenses, profitability and budget performance. However, the analyst's responsibility extends beyond displaying these metrics. The professional needs to identify unusual changes, recognise important trends and communicate their possible business significance. This is where business analytics becomes closely connected with Power BI. The technology helps present information, while analytical reasoning helps interpret it. Developing the Business Analytics Mindset Business analytics focuses on using data to understand organisational performance and support better decisions. An analyst may receive a requirement such as investigating declining sales. The solution could involve examining historical sales, customer segments, product categories, regional performance and marketing activity. The analyst may then use Power BI to visualise the findings and identify patterns. The final output should be more than a collection of charts. It should explain the evidence and highlight areas that deserve attention. This ability to connect technical analysis with business objectives is one of the most important capabilities learners can develop. Practical Projects and Real-World Application Projects provide an opportunity to combine multiple skills within one analytical workflow. A learner could work on a retail dataset and build a sales performance dashboard. The project might involve cleaning the data, creating a model, developing DAX measures, designing visualisations and presenting conclusions. Another project could focus on marketing analytics, where learners examine campaign performance, customer acquisition costs and conversion rates. These projects help learners understand how different components of analytics work together. They can also become part of a professional portfolio. A portfolio containing dashboards, analytical reports and case studies can demonstrate practical capability more effectively than a list of software names alone. This is particularly relevant in a skills-focused employment environment. The Economic Times reported in 2026 that Indian technology employers are increasingly emphasising practical AI capabilities and demonstrable skills, while a shortage of industry-ready talent remains a concern. Power BI, AI and the Future of Analytics Artificial intelligence is changing the way professionals interact with business data. AI-assisted tools can help automate repetitive activities, accelerate analysis and support users in exploring information. Power BI can increasingly be used alongside AI capabilities to make analytics more accessible and efficient. However, AI does not eliminate the need for analytical judgement. Professionals still need to determine whether the data is accurate, whether a pattern is meaningful and whether an automatically generated insight makes sense in the business context. Recent reporting from Moneycontrol indicates that employers are increasingly valuing workflow understanding, data skills and decision-making as enterprise AI adoption expands. Another Moneycontrol report highlighted the growing value of combining AI capabilities with existing analytical tools such as Power BI, with AI-assisted analytics emerging as an increasingly relevant workplace skill. This means future analytics professionals may benefit from learning both traditional analytical foundations and emerging AI-enabled workflows. Career Scope Across Industries Power BI and business analytics skills can be applied across a wide range of sectors. In banking and financial services, dashboards can help monitor financial performance, customer behaviour and operational metrics. In retail, analytics can support sales forecasting, inventory analysis, customer segmentation and product performance tracking. Marketing teams can use business intelligence to understand campaign results, customer acquisition and conversion rates. Healthcare organisations can apply analytics to operational performance, resource utilisation and reporting. Manufacturing and logistics businesses can use dashboards to monitor production, supply chains, inventory and delivery performance. This broad applicability creates several potential career directions, including Data Analyst, Business Intelligence Analyst, Business Analyst, Reporting Analyst, Marketing Analyst, Operations Analyst and BI Developer. A data analytics course in Kolkata can therefore provide learners with skills that are relevant beyond a single industry. As businesses adopt more digital systems, their ability to collect and analyse information continues to grow. This increases the relevance of professionals who can work with data and communicate business insights. items.title: HOW ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CAN SYSTEMATICALLY ENHANCE SOFT SKILLS IN ENGLISH BLENDED LEARNING – A PEDAGOGICAL DESIGN FOR CHINESE EFL LEARNERS
items.abstract: Soft skills are essential for university students, yet many Chinese EFL learners remain at a knowledge-telling stage, prioritizing language proficiency over interpreting acquired knowledge, while curriculum design has long centered on language hard skills with soft skills often not explicitly included as instructional objectives. This marginalization of soft skills is a persistent dilemma. Artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, is profoundly reshaping foreign language education and offering new possibilities for systematically cultivating soft skills. Nevertheless, current higher education English teaching faces two separate dilemmas: the marginalization of soft skills development, and the lack of standardization in AI use. This paper focuses on the first question of how artificial intelligence tools can systematically enhance university students’ soft skills within an English blended learning environment. This paper proposes a pedagogical design aiming to transform soft skills from implicit expectations into explicit instructional objectives.

items.title: How consumers process sustainability messages in a randomized two-wave experiment on household food waste reduction in Japan
items.abstract: Abstract Information campaigns are widely used to reduce household food waste, yet little is known about how consumers process the messages they receive. This study investigates whether differently framed messages trigger qualitatively different cognitive-moral responses and whether randomized message assignment changes self-reported outcomes. In a randomized two-wave experiment with Japanese consumers (Wave 1 n = 2069; Wave 2 n = 959, five-week follow-up), participants received information framed around tax burdens (Tax frame), global hunger (Hunger frame), household monetary costs (Cost frame), or a general-information control. Open-ended responses were classified into five Norm Activation Theory (NAT; [31]) stages using two independent large language model coders with researcher adjudication, supplemented by a blinded author re-coding exercise. Framing causally shifted message interpretation: the Tax and Hunger frames increased the probability of ascribing responsibility (+ 5.1 and + 5.8 percentage points), while the Cost frame uniquely elevated personal norm activation (+ 4.5 points). However, intention-to-treat estimates show no effects on self-reported preventive practices, normative orientation, or policy support. The one persistent effect is negative: five weeks later, the Tax frame reduced food waste reduction motivation (− 0.15 SD), a pattern consistent with motivational crowding-out, although the mechanism was not directly tested. Information framing changes cognitive-moral interpretation but not self-reported practices—a process-level distinction that helps explain the intention–behavior gap and informs the design of household sustainability communication.

items.title: How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk
items.abstract: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.

items.title: How High Is 0.6? Floors, Ceilings, and Headroom in Interpretability Probing
items.abstract: Probes are the workhorse of interpretability. If a model's hidden states predict a variable, the model is said to represent it. But a probe score has no fixed meaning. An $R^2$ of 0.6 may only reflect what the input already gives away, and the same score can mean different things on different data. We propose reading every probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. The gap between them, the headroom, is the range in which a probe can show that a model computes something beyond the simple inputs. We prove that headroom vanishes in two ways: the target stops depending on a hidden variable the model must infer, or the input stops revealing it. We test this on transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis, which must infer the hidden heterogeneity between studies to weight them correctly, and where both reference points are known. Under distribution shift, probe scores fall and prediction error rises $12$--$15\times$, yet the model recovers a similar share of the headroom, indicating that the data lost information, not the representation. We then analyze the real models. The single-cell foundation model scGPT encodes biological variability only partially. We also revisit four influential LLM probing studies, which claim that models represent geography, the state of an Othello board, truth, and the demographics of their users. Against a floor computed from the input text alone, some of these claims hold, while others are largely explained by the text itself.

items.title: How Learning Governs Unlearning across the Memorization-Generalization Spectrum
items.abstract: While unlearning seeks to negate undesired capabilities acquired through learning, little research has examined how the way models learn shapes their subsequent unlearning. In this paper, we investigate this connection from the perspectives of memorization and generalization, the two most representative yet competing strategies that models employ during training. We first classify memorization- and generalization-heavy models using grokking in modular addition and compare their responses to unlearning, showing that the latter suffer greater retain damage, i.e., a larger performance drop on the retain set. Furthermore, we conduct a finer-grained analysis by introducing bucketed modular addition, in which the respective contributions of the two strategies can be explicitly controlled across the memorization-generalization spectrum. In this setup, we reaffirm that the same trend persists and is nearly monotonic. We further demonstrate that this relationship also holds in LLM unlearning across verbatim and factual recall settings. Finally, we provide two practical insights for developing better unlearning methods, highlighting the importance of accounting for learning dynamics in unlearning.

items.title: How to Use This Book
items.abstract: This chapter provides an instructor-oriented guide to teaching Chinese politics in an era shaped by geopolitical tension, pedagogical transformation and the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education. It argues that teaching China today requires more than transmitting factual knowledge; it involves helping students navigate uncertainty, contested narratives, algorithmically mediated information environments and the methodological challenges of studying politics under conditions of partial visibility. The chapter outlines how the textbook&s;s modular structure, simulations, translation literacy tools, digital literacy exercises and “How Do We Know?” epistemic framework are designed to support flexible teaching across undergraduate, postgraduate and interdisciplinary contexts, while encouraging analytical reasoning, methodological reflexivity and inclusive participation. It also examines the implications of generative AI for assessment, authorship and critical thinking, arguing for pedagogical approaches that treat AI not simply as a threat to academic integrity but as an object of critical reflection and higher-order learning. In addition, the chapter situates the textbook within broader debates on inclusive curriculum design, decolonising knowledge production and diversifying perspectives in China studies, while emphasising comparative, interdisciplinary and student-centred approaches to learning. Overall, the chapter positions the study of Chinese politics as both an intellectual and pedagogical project that equips students to think critically about governance, knowledge, technology and power in an increasingly complex global environment.

items.title: How Well Do LLMs Reason with Noisy Evidence? An Active Visual Reasoning Benchmark
items.abstract: Real-world reasoning rarely reduces to static question answering: agents must actively gather information from tools and sensors that are often noisy and unreliable. Yet most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume that environmental feedback is trustworthy, or introduce noise without exposing an explicit, calibrated uncertainty signal, leaving open how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. We introduce VisualNoiseQA, a novel benchmark for active reasoning under noisy visual feedback. A text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, we draw multiple samples and expose an empirical uncertainty signal via self-consistency, enabling the reasoner to probe from different angles and decide what to ask next and when to stop. Our construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, we retain only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable. We evaluate multiple LLM reasoners on 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. VisualNoiseQA thus provides a controlled playground to study how different LLMs exploit uncertainty signals for robust reasoning.

items.title: HSV-Net: hybrid state-space and self-supervised vision fusion with progressive contour learning for CT pulmonary nodule segmentation
items.abstract: Accurate voxel-level segmentation of pulmonary nodules on chest CT is needed for diameter and volume measurement, growth tracking, and quantitative assessment in lung cancer screening. The task remains difficult: nodules vary in attenuation, size, and contact with vessels or pleura, and clinically relevant morphology often lies in a thin, ambiguous margin. Existing systems commonly trade contour fidelity for speed—large prompt-driven foundation models can be accurate but slow, whereas compact CNN or SSM decoders are efficient yet tend to smooth spiculated and ground-glass borders. We propose HSV-Net (Hybrid State-space–Vision Network), a dual-stream 3D network that is prompt-free after nodule localization: an SSM3D stream provides whole-patch context with linear-complexity state-space blocks, and an OrthoLoRA stream adapts frozen DINOv2 features on axial, coronal, and sagittal slices. A Hybrid Gated Mixer (HGM) fuses the two streams before FPN decoding, and Progressive Contour Learning (PCL) supervises overlap, signed-distance-field geometry, and uncertainty-weighted contour refinement. On a 10-patient QIN Lung CT/QIN-LungCT-Seg development subset ( n = 12 tumors; nested patient-level 5-fold CV), HSV-Net obtained the highest mean Dice (90.1% ± 1.0%; 95% CI [88.9, 91.3]) and Boundary F1 (86.3% ± 1.3%) among the compared methods on 128 × 128 × 64 patches, with a latency of 58 ms. A standard full-volume nnU-Net v2 baseline reached 88.6% ± 1.0% Dice on the same QIN folds, still below HSV-Net. On an independent LIDC-IDRI benchmark with expert volumetric consensus masks (186 patients/294 nodules; patient-level 5-fold CV within LIDC, not QIN→LIDC transfer), HSV-Net achieved 87.8% ± 1.1% Dice and 83.6% ± 1.3% Boundary F1, outperforming full-volume nnU-Net (87.1% ± 1.0% Dice). LUNA16 was retained only as a proxy size/localization check with diameter-matched spherical references, not as contour external validation.

items.title: Human Resource Development in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Common Good Approach
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming how and under what conditions employees learn, work, and develop their careers. This has strong implications for human resource development (HRD), because AI goes beyond technology itself and presents social and ethical issues concerning whose capabilities are recognized, whose learning is supported, and whose career futures are protected. In this paper, we develop a perspective on HRD in the era of AI through a common good lens. A common good approach to HRD not only supports employees vulnerable to job displacement by providing them with skills and mindsets beneficial for their sustainable employment and careers, but also contributes to society by developing human capital and a sustainable labor force, as well as enhancing the wellbeing of the workers and their families. This approach requires organizations to balance both efficiency and human relationships and align organizational goals (economic and social) with common good outcomes for individuals and society. It transforms HRD from a traditional HRM function into a dynamic, justice‐based, relationship‐oriented, and sustainability‐driven system. We outline several new research avenues to advance the HRD field through a common‐good lens.

items.title: Human Resources Control System
items.abstract: Organizations utilize human resources (HR) control as a vital mechanism for managing employee performance and ensuring that individual contributions align with company objectives. The earlier research documented HR control functions through three primary approaches: behavioral, output and input control. Behavioral control monitors and regulates employee behavior through established procedures, guidelines and oversight that dictate how tasks should be performed. Output control shifts the focus to outcomes by assessing employees based on measurable results, such as productivity, sales or service quality. In contrast, input control aims to enhance employee capabilities through skill development, training and ongoing education, ensuring that individuals possess the necessary competencies to perform effectively. By linking traditional control mechanisms to organizational strategy, incentive design and performance evaluation, contemporary HRM methods enhance their effectiveness. Modern HR control systems aim not only to regulate behavior but also to promote high levels of employee commitment, engagement and ownership of performance. This chapter distinguishes between control-based and commitment-based HR approaches. Control-based systems emphasize compliance and monitoring, while commitment-based systems nurture empowerment, trust and intrinsic motivation. The challenge for modern organizations is to develop HR systems that enforce accountability without undermining employee autonomy and organizational citizenship. The chapter argues that HR control systems must evolve beyond the traditional dimensions of behavior, output and input by incorporating Porter’s three strategic orientations: cost leadership, differentiation and focus. For example, a differentiation strategy would necessitate a greater emphasis on innovation, empowerment and talent development. In contrast, a cost leadership strategy may require more stringent performance metrics and productivity controls. Consequently, HR control systems should be tailored to align with an organization’s specific strategic choices, culture and environment. Human control is not a one-size-fits-all strategy, as suggested by global best practices. Leading companies develop context-specific HR control frameworks that integrate data analytics, technology, competence mapping and adaptable performance systems. These approaches cultivate the commitment essential for sustained high performance while ensuring accountability. Ultimately, the key to effective HR control lies in creating an ecosystem where freedom and structure coexist to enhance organizational excellence.

items.title: Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models
items.abstract: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

items.title: Humanoid AI with Humanity Modeling: Bridging Humans and Virtual–Physical Humanoids
items.abstract: The seventy-year AI is now entering another major resurgence, the era of Generative AI (GenAI), characterized by the rapid advancement of large multimodal models (LMMs). GenAI and LMMs are fundamentally transforming sixty-decade-old humanoid robots, advancing them from human-looking and humanlike embodiments toward human-level AI and robotics, and inspiring a new era of AI-robotics symbiosis: humanoid AI . Humanoid AI develops humane AI-driven humanoids (AI humanoids) that go beyond traditional human-looking robots, which typically exhibit little or no humanity and intelligence due to their dedication to predefined and limited AI functions and exteriors. By contrast, AI humanoids undertake real-time, situated, and interactive mind-to-action, perception-to-behavior, and vision-to-emotion transformations, achieving an unprecedented degree of replicating human characteristics and intelligence. Realizing this vision requires systematic humanity modeling, ensuring that AI humanoids are shaped, guided, and governed by robust frameworks of AI and robotic humanity. We then propose human-virtual-physical humanoid transform and alignment and human-metaverse-humanoid ecosystem for open, complex human-digital-machine-cooperative methodology and problem-solving, followed by general principles and frameworks for building actionable humanoids and evaluating humanoid quality.

items.title: HygieneRoboBench: Benchmarking Hygiene-Aware Planning for Household Robots
items.abstract: Contact with contaminated objects can spread hazards through a household robot's grippers, tools, and shared surfaces, while new contacts can make an existing plan unsafe. Existing benchmarks do not jointly assess how planners identify hygiene risks from contact history and plan safe continuations after new contact events. Planners must do so within time and resource limits while respecting user priorities. We introduce HygieneRoboBench, with 624 instances across 134 task families, to evaluate safe resolution of household tasks from a given execution history. Tasks capture contamination through two grippers and shared objects, treatment costs, and user priorities. We combine controlled history, profile, and event comparisons with independent plan evaluation. These assess safe resolution, cost efficiency under user priorities, and responses to contact events. Evaluation of LLM-based and symbolic planners shows that safely completing a task does not guarantee the lowest execution costs under the user's priorities. To address this problem, we introduce Hygiene-NSP. It combines LLM-based grounding, contact-history reconstruction, and CP-SAT to jointly plan hygiene treatment and task execution under user priorities. Hygiene-NSP achieves safe resolution and optimal safe resolution rates of 94.4% and 90.4%, respectively. Both rates are higher than those of the evaluated baseline planners on the full dataset. Project page: https://euron-zc.github.io/HygieneRoboBench/.

items.title: IdeaAnchor: Teaching LLMs to Turn Literature into Research Ideas
items.abstract: Scientific research often begins by synthesizing ideas from a set of related papers to identify gaps and formulate new directions. However, training language models to perform this form of literature-grounded ideation remains challenging, as existing approaches based on prompting or feedback lack structured supervision for how papers should be synthesized. We introduce IdeaAnchor, a paradigm for training LLMs to perform research ideation using structured specifications as privileged signals. Each IdeaAnchor instance encodes how each input paper should be synthesized into a successful idea, including their functional roles, relationships, and target synthesis criteria. We build this paradigm by mining instances from published papers, capturing how real ideas emerge from prior literature. We then train models via demonstration, self-distillation, and reinforcement learning, and further enhance generation with retrieval at inference time. Experiments show consistent improvements in ideation quality. Our analysis reveals a functional decomposition: anchor-based training strengthens creative synthesis, retrieval enhances detail elaboration, and combining both yields the best performance.

items.title: Identity Threat as a Barrier to NHS Psychology Professionals’ Adoption of Generative AI: A Technology Acceptance Model Study
items.abstract: Introduction. The development and adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies is rapidly expanding, but its integration into psychological services depends on clinician acceptance. Little empirical work has examined how identity-related threat shapes psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI. The present research tested an extended technology acceptance model (TAM), with the addition of personal and professional identity threats, to explain psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI technologies for clinically relevant usage. Methods. A total of 201 UK psychology professionals completed a cross-sectional online survey. Three sequential structural equation models were tested, incorporating perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and social influence as core predictors, with threats to professional capabilities and self-threat added as extensions. Two open-ended qualitative questions were analysed using content analysis to provide broader contextual insight into current use and barriers to adoption. Results. All models demonstrated acceptable fit (CFI = 0.936–0.938; RMSEA = 0.071–0.072). Perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest correlate of adoption intention across all models (β = 0.67–0.69). Threats to professional capabilities and self-threat were each reliably negatively associated with adoption intention when entered separately, above and beyond core TAM predictors (β = −0.20 and β = −0.16 respectively). Social influence exerted a reliable indirect effect on behavioural intention through perceived usefulness across all models, as did perceived ease of use in the two models incorporating identity threat. Content analysis identified ethical concerns, lack of trust, and professional identity threats as prominent barriers to adoption. Discussion. Findings highlight the importance of considering both classic TAM factors and identity-related concerns when developing GenAI and implementing such technology into psychological services.

items.title: Illusory Pattern Perception Drives Spurious Inference in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Illusory pattern perception is a well-documented human cognitive tendency to infer meaningful relationships in data that is actually random. Such a tendency, often described as "connecting the dots" where none exist, can result in systematic reasoning errors. This paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit such perceptual tendencies, which can lead to systematic errors in downstream applications. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of illusory pattern perception in LLMs, adapting classic psychological paradigms to three tasks with direct empirical comparison to human behaviors. We find that LLMs frequently exhibit stronger illusory pattern perception than humans. In particular, models tend to over-associate frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations, and show increased tendencies to construct causal narratives from ambiguous events. To uncover the mechanism behind these behaviors, we develop a feature interpretability framework based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to analyze internal representations. Our results reveal that holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation are linked to the emergence of illusory perceptions. These findings highlight a previously underexplored cognitive-like illusion that may affect the reliability of LLM reasoning. Code available at https://github.com/NusIoraPrivacy/illusory.

items.title: Image Quality Assessment in Chest Radiography According to European Guidelines: A Narrative Review of Its Relevance and Implementation Challenges in Cameroon
items.abstract: Abstract: Chest radiography remains the cornerstone of diagnostic imaging globally,functioning as a primary triage and diagnostic tool for a diverse array of cardiopulmonarypathologies, particularly tuberculosis and pneumonia. In resource-constrained environments likeCameroon, healthcare systems exhibit an extreme reliance on chest radiography; however, thestructural frameworks necessary to optimize image quality and minimize patient radiation doseare frequently inadequate. This narrative review evaluates the clinical relevance and practicalimplementation of stringent European image quality guidelines specifically the EUR 16260anatomical criteria and the European Union Directive 2013/59/Euratom within theCameroonian context. The analysis synthesizes current methods of image quality assessment,encompassing visual grading analysis, reject and repeat audits, standardized exposure indices(IEC 62494-1), and the integration of artificial intelligence tools such as CAD4TB. TranslatingEuropean standards to Cameroon encounters profound structural barriers, driven primarily by acritical shortage of radiological personnel, with a radiologist density of approximately two permillion inhabitants compared to the European average of 127 per million. Additional frictionpoints include the unmonitored transition from analogue to digital radiography, the inconsistentapplication of Diagnostic Reference Levels (DRLs), and the limited enforcement capacity of theNational Radiation Protection Agency (ANRP). Despite these systemic hurdles, strategicopportunities exist to elevate diagnostic standards. Expanding teleradiology networks to supportremote facilities, implementing low-cost quality assurance audits, and leveraging artificialintelligence for automated image assessment offer viable solutions to bridge the quality gap.The establishment of localized DRLs and the prioritized training of radiographers and medicalphysics experts stand as essential prerequisites for achieving sustainable diagnostic excellenceand radiation safety in Cameroon. Establishing routine diagnostic reference levels for standardprocedures is a universally recommended practice for adhering strictly to the ALARA principle.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Fraud Prevention on Customer Trust in Digital Payment Systems: An Empirical Investigation of Continuance Intention among Indian Users
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems in India, anchored by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), has been accompanied by a sharp rise in payment fraud, eroding consumer confidence and threatening long-term adoption. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fraud prevention mechanisms—real-time anomaly detection, behavioural biometrics, and adaptive authentication—are increasingly deployed by payment service providers to mitigate this risk. Drawing on the Expectation-Confirmation Model of Information Systems Continuance (Bhattacherjee, 2001) and the trust literature (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995), this study empirically examines the influence of perceived AI security features on customers' continuance intention toward digital payment applications. A cross-sectional survey of 350 active digital payment users in India was conducted using a structured, five-point Likert-scale instrument. Pearson correlation analysis revealed a very strong, positive, and statistically significant association between AI security features and continuance intention (r = .900, p < .001, 95% CI [.878, .918]). Simple linear regression confirmed that AI security features significantly predict continuance intention, explaining 76.7% of the variance (R² = .767, F(1, 348) = 1147.00, p < .001; β = .876, t = 33.87, p < .001). The findings substantiate the proposition that visible, intelligent fraud-prevention capabilities function as a salient trust-building cue, thereby reinforcing users' decision to continue using digital payment platforms. The paper discusses theoretical and managerial implications, acknowledges limitations, and outlines directions for future research.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Clinicians’ Diagnostic and Management Decisions for Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules on CT
items.abstract: Indeterminate pulmonary nodules (IPNs) detected on computed tomography (CT) pose challenges because malignancy risk assessment is essential to balance early cancer detection with unnecessary invasive procedures. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used as a decision-support tool for pulmonary nodule assessment, but its impact on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions remains less established than the performance of AI algorithms. This systematic review evaluated the effect of AI assistance on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions for CT-detected IPNs. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from 2015 to 2026. Eligible studies assessed AI-assisted evaluation of indeterminate or suspicious pulmonary nodules on CT, involved clinicians, and reported diagnostic or management outcomes. Five retrospective reader-study or multireader multicase studies were included. AI assistance improved diagnostic performance and malignancy risk stratification. One study reported an AUC increase from 0.82 to 0.89 (P<0.001), with higher sensitivity, specificity, and interobserver agreement (Fleiss κ, 0.35 to 0.58; P<0.001). Another found sensitivity increased from 60% to 98% and specificity from 69% to 99%. Among advanced practice providers, AUC increased from 0.79 to 0.88, while invasive procedure recommendations for malignant nodules increased from 55% to 72%. AI detection also benefited radiologists across experience levels. Standalone AI performed worse than experienced radiologists. AI may improve clinician performance and management decisions, especially as a second-reader tool. Evidence remains limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous systems and outcomes, and lack of randomized trials; prospective studies are needed.

items.abstract: Digital Education and Future Learning Ecosystem: Impact on Students' Academic Achievement in the 21st Century Digital Education and Future Learning Ecosystem: Impact on Students' Academic Achievement in the 21st Century In the 21st century, Education has experienced a huge paradigm shift from the traditional chalk-and-talk way of learning to technologically created learning ecosystems. The COVID-19 pandemic brought a global revolution in bringing in Digital Education. Digital India, SWAYAM, DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA and NEP- 2020 all emphasise the role of technology in education in the Indian context. The present research paper is an effort to critically examine the impact of "Digital Education and Future Learning Ecosystem viz., e-learning platforms, Artificial Intelligence in Education (AiE) and Virtual Classrooms, on learners' academic achievement. It is primarily a descriptive and analytical study based on secondary data collected from various scholarly published papers, UNESCO reports, Reports of UGC, NEP 2020, etc. (2020-2025). The outcome of study suggested that Digital Education has a significant positive impact on Learners' Academic Achievement through personalised learning, flexibility and flexibility, accessibility, audio-visual contents and involvement, personalised learning technology and AI-based adaptive learning platforms leading to enhancement of learning outcomes by 20-30%. But the digital divide, absence of social interaction, digital fatigue and deficiency of teachers' digital skills pose challenges. The paper concludes with a suggestion that integrating both learning styles is the best sustainable future learning ecosystem for Indian Education in the context of 21st Century. The study will help all the stakeholders, viz., policymakers, educators, educational institutions etc.

items.title: IMPLICATIONS AND INSTRUCTIONAL RESPONSES TO AI-RELATED COGNITIVE OUTSOURCING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: This article addresses the phenomenon of cognitive outsourcing in foreign language education amid the rapid proliferation of generative AI tools. Cognitive outsourcing is defined as the deliberate transfer of cognitively demanding language-learning tasks to AI systems in ways that bypass the mental processing necessary for skill development and knowledge acquisition. The study distinguishes it from legitimate uses of AI, arguing that the key criterion is whether AI involvement occurs before or after the cognitive engagement with a task. The article examines six domains in which cognitive outsourcing manifests: essay writing, vocabulary acquisition, conversational practice with AI chatbots, grammar learning, translation, and preparation for oral performance tasks. The analysis shows how AI-mediated shortcuts undermine mechanisms of second language acquisition, including generative processing in writing, productive inference in vocabulary learning, negotiation in conversation, the noticing process in grammar development, desirable difficulty in reading comprehension, and spontaneous communication in oral production. Particular attention is given to the motivational consequences of outsourcing - erosion of learners’ ideal L2 self and long-term engagement. Rejecting a prohibitionist stance toward AI as pedagogically counterproductive, the article proposes the cultivation of cognitive outsourcing awareness. This approach is presented as essential for three reasons: learners rarely recognize outsourcing dynamics without guidance; the concept offers a constructive, nonadversarial discussing AI use in the classroom; and explicit instruction addresses equity concerns, since learners with weaker metacognitive and critical literacy skills are vulnerable to uncritical AI dependence. The article concludes that fostering informed, reflective AI use offers the most viable path for preserving the developmental benefits of effortful language learning while acknowledging the realities of a technology-saturated educational environment

items.title: Improving Synthetic Data Generation for Argument Mining via Adversarial Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Argument Mining (AM) is fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of high-quality structure-annotated datasets. While LLMs have shown promise in synthetic data generation, producing synthetic AM data that is both structurally accurate and sufficiently diverse remains a challenging problem. To address this problem, we revisit synthetic data generation for AM from a new perspective and propose a novel adversarial reinforcement learning framework for data synthesis. The proposed framework jointly optimizes the generator and the discriminator in an adversarial loop, in which the generator produces structured AM instances, and the discriminator provides learning signals by distinguishing real data from synthetic candidates. This enables the generator to progressively improve both the structural accuracy of generated argument data while maintaining diversity through adversarial feedback. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves AM performance on three benchmark datasets in both full-data and low-resource settings, validating its effectiveness and scalability.

items.title: INFLUENCE OF AI-POWERED MARKETING ON CONSUMER ENGAGEMENT AND BRAND LOYALTY
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a working part of everyday marketing rather than a futuristic idea. Brands now use AI for personalised recommendations, chatbots, predictive analytics and automated content, and this is changing the way customers interact with them. This paper looks at how AI-powered marketing affects two closely linked outcomes: consumer engagement (how actively and how often customers interact with a brand) and brand loyalty (how likely they are to stay with a brand and keep buying from it). Since collecting fresh primary data was not possible for this paper, the study relies entirely on secondary data drawn from industry reports, survey findings published by research firms, and existing academic literature on AI and marketing. The analysis shows that AI-driven personalisation, chatbots and predictive tools generally raise engagement and can strengthen loyalty, but only when they are used with a reasonable amount of transparency and human judgement. Where AI is used carelessly, or where customers feel their data is being misused, the same tools that are meant to build loyalty can just as easily damage trust. The paper ends with practical suggestions for marketers, a note on the limitations of a secondary-data study, and directions that future researchers could explore, particularly through primary, first-hand data collection.

items.title: Innovations in Microsurgery: A Qualitative Appraisal of a Novel 3D-Printed Microscope
items.abstract: Background Microsurgery is a critical component of plastic and reconstructive surgery. However, the high cost of training and equipment pose significant barriers, particularly in resource-limited settings. To address this challenge, the Microsurgery and Regenerative Medicine Lab within the Division of Plastic Surgery at the University of Wisconsin developed a low-cost, 3D-printed surgical microscope. This study qualitatively appraised the use of this novel microscope for microsurgery training by surveying surgeons about their experiences using this tool relative to traditional magnification methods. Methods In this prospective, multi-institutional appraisal study, surgical residents, fellows, and attending surgeons with varying microsurgical experience performed a single end-to-end microsurgical anastomosis on chicken thigh femoral arteries using the 3D-printed microscope. Participants then completed a survey assessing ease of use, adequacy for microsurgical training, educational value, and perceived impact on teaching capacity in local and global settings. Results Over 80% of participants reported that performing an end-to-end anastomosis was easier or equivalent using the 3D-printed microscope compared to surgical loupes. Additionally, 91.7% (33/36) believed access to the microscope would enhance microsurgical teaching at their home institutions, and 97.1% (34/35) felt it would improve teaching capacity in globally. Qualitative feedback was overwhelmingly positive, with suggestions primarily related to ergonomics and lighting. Conclusion This study supports that this low-cost, 3D-printed microscope is an effective microsurgical training tool. Ongoing design refinements informed by user feedback may further optimize its role in expanding access to microsurgery education worldwide.
